# The Publicist as Institutional Infrastructure — complete editable platform copy

## 1. LONG VIDEO
Start with the image everyone saw, then open the hidden stack: frame, proof, relationship, access, permission, spokesperson, approval, disclosure, correction, and archive. Use Lambert to show field-building and the public agreement to show negotiated governance.

## 2. SHORT 01
“A publicist does not merely get attention. A publicist helps decide what becomes legible.” End with the accountability question: whose labor and evidence made the frame possible?

## 3. SHORT 02
“Coverage is an output. Institutional memory is the release, approval, correction, refusal, permission, and relationship record behind it.”

## 4. CAROUSEL
THE STORY / THE PROOF / THE AUDIENCE / THE RELATIONSHIP / THE ACCESS / THE APPROVAL / THE DISCLOSURE / THE CREDIT / THE CORRECTION / THE ARCHIVE.

## 5. NEWSLETTER
Subject: Publicity is infrastructure when the receipts survive. Distinguish field-building, campaign work, media relations, and archive practice without treating one famous career as universal.

## 6. PRESS-ROOM EDITION
A live claim-and-permission board for release copy, biographies, quotes, product assertions, images, credits, spokespersons, embargoes, disclosures, and corrections.

## Claim ledger
- **VERIFIED:** The Museum at FIT describes Eleanor Lambert as a fashion publicist whose long practice advocated for American designers and the New York fashion industry. (S79)
- **VERIFIED:** FIT preserves Lambert’s papers and records in a collection organized around her professional activities and institutions. (S80)
- **VERIFIED:** A public Estée Lauder consulting agreement expressly addresses specified services, approvals, publicity materials, media, and uses of persona; it is evidence of one negotiated allocation, not a universal PR arrangement. (S78)

## Publication discipline
Use the copy as written with the package's rendered social artwork. Preserve captions, alt text, creator and institution credits, canonical URLs, evidence labels, labor and jurisdiction limits, participant correction, and counsel or specialist boundaries.
